title: LongAdder: striped cells, reduces contention vs AtomicLong, when to prefer
keyPoints: LongAdder (Java 8) reduces CAS contention by striping: instead of all threads CAS-ing one variable, each thread increments its own cell in a padded array.
Under low contention (1-2 threads), LongAdder falls back to a single base variable, performing identically to AtomicLong.
Under high contention (16+ threads), LongAdder is 5-10x faster than AtomicLong because each thread CAS-es its own cell with minimal contention.
sum() returns base plus all cells but is NOT an atomic snapshot: concurrent increments may produce a slightly stale sum.
Each Cell is annotated with @Contended to prevent false sharing between cells on adjacent cache lines.
Use LongAdder for high-write counters and metrics where exact real-time value is not needed; use AtomicLong when get() must return the exact current value.
LongAccumulator generalizes LongAdder: new LongAccumulator(Math::max, 0) tracks the maximum across threads using the same striping technique.

s1_definition.oneliner: LongAdder distributes increments across per-thread striped cells to eliminate CAS contention, achieving 5-10x higher throughput than AtomicLong under high contention, at the cost of a non-atomic sum().
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Striping** – instead of all threads competing to CAS a single shared counter (AtomicLong), LongAdder maintains an array of `Cell` objects. Each thread hashes to its own cell and CAS-es locally.
- **Adaptive** – under low contention, LongAdder uses a single `base` variable (just like AtomicLong). When a CAS on base fails (contention detected), the thread is assigned a Cell and increments that instead.
- **@Contended cells** – each Cell is annotated with `@Contended`, placing it on its own cache line (128-byte padding) to prevent false sharing.
- **Non-atomic sum()** – `sum()` reads `base + cells[0].value + cells[1].value + ...` without holding any lock. Concurrent increments during the sum may be missed, producing a slightly stale result.
- **LongAccumulator** – generalizes LongAdder with a custom accumulator function. `new LongAccumulator(Math::max, 0)` tracks the maximum value seen across all threads, using the same striping technique.
s1_definition.analogy: AtomicLong is like one shared click counter at the entrance to National Bank of India. When 100 customers arrive simultaneously, they all fight over the same button (CAS retry). LongAdder is like 10 separate counters at 10 different doors. Each customer clicks the nearest counter with no fighting. At the end of the day, the manager walks around and adds up all 10 counters. No fighting means 10x faster. But while the manager is adding, someone might click another counter, so the sum is slightly off, which is fine for daily totals but not for real-time account balances.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  LongAdder: Striped Cells
  ═══════════════════════

  AtomicLong (contention):
  Thread-1 ──→ CAS(base) ← fail, retry
  Thread-2 ──→ CAS(base) ← fail, retry
  Thread-3 ──→ CAS(base) ← fail, retry
  All threads fight over ONE variable!

  LongAdder (striped):
  Thread-1 ──→ CAS(cell[0])  ← success
  Thread-2 ──→ CAS(cell[1])  ← success
  Thread-3 ──→ CAS(cell[2])  ← success
  Each thread has its own cell!

  sum() = base + cell[0] + cell[1] + cell[2]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
LongAdder achieves 5-10x higher throughput than AtomicLong under high contention by distributing increments across per-thread striped cells. Each Cell is @Contended to prevent false sharing. Under low contention, it behaves identically to AtomicLong by using a single base variable. The trade-off is that sum() is not an atomic snapshot: it reads base and all cells without locking, so concurrent increments may produce a slightly stale total.

Use LongAdder for high-write counters, metrics, and rate limiters where the exact real-time value is not critical. Use AtomicLong when you need an exact value after each operation, such as account balances or sequence numbers. LongAccumulator extends the pattern to custom functions like Math::max for tracking maximums across threads.

At National Bank of India, the API gateway request counter using AtomicLong consumed 15% CPU under 200 concurrent threads due to CAS contention. Switching to LongAdder reduced CPU usage to under 1%, with sum() called once per second for the Grafana monitoring dashboard.

Remember one sentence: LongAdder stripes increments across per-thread cells to eliminate CAS contention, making it 5-10x faster than AtomicLong for counters that do not need exact real-time reads.
